approachQuestion.prompt:
Four mounting holes

Given four integer-coordinate points in arbitrary order, return whether they are the four distinct vertices of a square with positive area. Rotated squares are allowed; repeated points must return false.

Example 1: [(0,1),(1,0),(2,1),(1,2)] -> true.
Example 2: [(0,0),(2,0),(2,1),(0,1)] -> false.
Example 3: [(0,0),(0,0),(1,1),(1,1)] -> false.

Constraints and assumptions: Exactly four points are provided, each coordinate in [-10^6,10^6]. Do not change their input order. Use exact integer calculations and return a boolean. Choose the best time bound among the offered correct methods, then the least auxiliary storage when time ties.

options.text: Compute and locally sort all six squared distances. Require the four smallest to equal one positive d and the final two to equal 2d.
options.feedback: The pattern gives four equal sides and two equal diagonals with the square ratio. A positive d excludes coincident points; using all pairs makes input order irrelevant.

options.text: Compute all six squared distances and accept when the largest two are equal and positive, ignoring the other four.
options.feedback: The 2-by-1 rectangle has two equal largest diagonals but is not a square.

options.text: Accept only if there are exactly two distinct x values and two distinct y values with equal horizontal and vertical spans and all four combinations occur.
options.feedback: This recognizes axis-aligned squares but rejects the valid rotated square [(0,1),(1,0),(2,1),(1,2)].

options.text: Use the listed order as a cycle and accept if its four edge squared lengths are equal, including zero.
options.feedback: Four identical points pass the edge-equality test, although the required square must have positive area and distinct vertices.

feedback.reason: Recognize an unordered nondegenerate square through its complete distance multiset.
details: Compute the six pairwise squared distances into a fixed six-entry local array. Sort that local array with insertion sort. Accept exactly when it is [d,d,d,d,2d,2d] with d>0.

A square has four equal positive side distances and two equal diagonals twice that squared distance. Require d>0 to reject coincident points. Using all six unordered distances avoids depending on input vertex order.

complexityQuestion.prompt: Analyze only the revealed method (six-distance-pattern). Let C be the maximum absolute coordinate magnitude. There are always exactly four points and six distances. Choose its tightest standard worst-case time and auxiliary-space pair.
constraints: Exact signed 64-bit integer arithmetic, casting before calculations; arithmetic and comparisons cost one unit. No arbitrary-precision operations.
Iterative method, no recursion or hashing, no input copies. Auxiliary space includes all temporary state and buffers, excluding supplied input and returned output.
Include initialization and any copying; no hidden preprocessing or cache.

feedback.reason: Six distance calculations and sorting six values are constant-sized work.
details: Six pair distances and sorting exactly six entries require a fixed bound on operations. The six-entry array is auxiliary but constant in size; copying four point coordinates would also be constant, though not needed. Squared distances are at most 8*10^12 and twice a distance remains within signed 64-bit.

“O(1) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: Correct: both the point count and local distance array size are fixed.
“O(log(C + 1)) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: Word-cost distance arithmetic does not loop over coordinate magnitude.
“O(C + 1) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: The method does not enumerate possible coordinates.
